newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka to double thermal power generation capacity.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka to double thermal power generation capacity.

text.p: Sri Lanka will more than double thermal electricity generation capacity by June and the onset of intermonsoon showers means it is unlikely to impose further limits on use of grid power, officials said on Friday.
If the country is forced to run the new thermal plants, it will mean doubling diesel imports, a Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) official said.
"It all depends on rainfall," he added. "We'll run the new thermal plants only in a worst-case scenario."
Sri Lanka imported 600,000 tonnes of diesel last year, up from the planned 300,000 tonnes because of increased use of thermal power due to drought.

Water levels in the Indian Ocean island's depleted hydropower reservoirs had held steady with the onset of intermonsoon showers, he said, despite widespread fears of a repeat of last year's drought and powercuts of up to eight hours a day.
"We now have 241 gigawatt hours, about 19 percent of our storage, in the hydropower reservoirs, roughly the same level as at the start of April," the CEB official said.
"It seems that this time we'll have no problems except for the restrictions already imposed to conserve electricity," he said.
The government this month banned the use of air-conditioners operating on the national grid and urged private sector businesses to use their own generators.

The restrictions were imposed after water levels in the hydro-reservoirs, which supply 85 percent of grid power, plunged to dangerously low levels with the failure of the northeast monsoon and the delayed onset of intermonsoon showers.
Sri Lanka has two rainy seasons. The southwest monsoon, the most important for fuelling hydroelectric plants, usually starts around the third week of May.
A Meteorology Department official said this year's southwest monsoon was expected on time.

"Until then, we'll get evening thunder showers, although not every day," deputy director P. M. Jayatilaka Banda told Reuters. "We expect the monsoon by the third week of May or by the end of May. It is still too early to say exactly when."
The CEB has said it plans to cut dependence on hydropower to 57 percent of the electricity requirement by building more thermal power plants and buying electricity from private plants.
The island now has an installed capacity of 1,135 megawatts of hydropower and 250 megawatts of thermal power.
"We've already added 80 megawatts from private plants and will add 50 megawatts more shortly," the CEB official said.
A 115-megawatt gas turbine and a 40-megawatt diesel plant would be ready by June, he said.
